stories.summary: After Chernobyl, many people could explain the disaster away as Soviet stupidity: an oppressive system where people feared being sent to Siberia kept making wrong decisions, and a liberal democracy would do better. Fukushima in 2011 ended that comfort. Angela Merkel, who has a PhD in chemistry and could reason about probabilities, called a meeting around one sentence: the Japanese are as good as us, so if it happened there, can it happen here? Germans saw themselves as better engineers than the Soviets but not better than the Japanese. Germany then decided to shut down all its nuclear power, which Ajay says looks like a poor decision from where we sit in 2024.
stories.insight: Even scientifically literate leaders can be moved by who an accident happened to rather than by base rates. Germany's U-turn came from a shaken sense of 'it could be us', not from new data about nuclear safety.
stories.quote: So if an accident could happen in Japan, could it happen in Germany?

stories.topic: Beating the U-boats with Assembly-Line Ships
stories.summary: In 1941 German U-boats were sinking the transport ships that carried food and military supplies from America to Britain, and hundreds of ships were lost. Ships had always been artisanal products, each one built piece by piece and each slightly different. The Americans took a mediocre British design of about 10,000 tons, nicknamed the 'ugly duckling', and mass-produced it Henry Ford style at 18 shipyards. As the yards learned, the time to commission a ship fell from 270 days to 35. About 2,700 ships were built and the price fell sharply. Germany could not sink ships as fast as American manufacturing could make them.
stories.insight: Scale and the learning curve beat craftsmanship. Ajay uses this story to explain why nuclear power can become cheap: build small reactors on assembly lines instead of one-off giant plants.
stories.quote: So that approach to the Germans was yeah, you keep shooting down our ships, we'll make even more of the ships.

stories.summary: The German Tiger tank was a great tank, but it was built by master craftsmen, and the design changed after every eleven tanks. That pushed costs up. The Americans mass-produced Sherman tanks on assembly lines, taught the Soviets to do the same with the T-34, and together they outproduced German manufacturing by about ten times.
stories.insight: Constant tinkering by experts is the enemy of cost reduction. A standardised, good-enough design that can be produced at volume wins wars, and markets.
stories.quote: Every eleven tiger tanks that were produced, there would be a change in the design. Because the people making those tanks were master craftsmen. And that's dumb.

stories.topic: India's 1974 Nuclear Test, Built from Scratch
stories.summary: Most nuclear powers got there through leaks. The Soviets stole secrets from the Manhattan Project, the Soviets passed knowledge to China, and China passed it to North Korea and Pakistan. India went from scratch to a nuclear test in 1974 entirely on its own. Ajay credits Homi Bhabha, Raja Ramanna, Sethna and their colleagues. He then separates that achievement from the problem of cheap nuclear electricity, which is an ordinary industrial problem closer to Bharat Heavy Electricals and a poor fit for the Indian state.
stories.insight: Being good at a strategic science project is different from being good at efficient, scaled industry. Treating civilian power as an extension of the bomb programme is why India's nuclear energy share has stayed tiny.
stories.quote: India is one of the few countries which figured this out entirely alone. Whereas in most of the other nuclear powers, somebody or the other leaked information to them.

stories.topic: The Numbers That Didn't Add Up at the Finance Ministry
stories.summary: When Ajay was at the Ministry of Finance, he ran early calculations on India's government-run nuclear plants. The conclusion was that, once costs were measured properly, they could never play a meaningful role in India's energy mix. Top-of-the-line French and American reactors were far more cost-efficient than what was being built in India.
stories.insight: The problem with Indian nuclear power was never only fear of accidents. The state-monopoly model simply could not deliver competitive economics.
stories.quote: I had started on some early calculations that this isn't going anywhere.

stories.topic: When Fear Itself Kills: Fukushima and 9/11
stories.summary: Amit recalls Ajay's point, made before recording, that after Fukushima the reactors were shut down and Japan shifted to coal, and that switch caused deaths. He adds a fact he half-remembers: after 9/11, tighter security and fear led people to fly less and drive more. Car accidents kill far more people than plane crashes, so mortality went up.
stories.insight: Refusing a technology does not mean choosing zero risk. It means accepting the risks of whatever replaces it. Not using nuclear power has a body count too.
stories.quote: So actually it wasn't the nuclear energy per se or that accident that caused deaths. It was then stopping to use it, getting carried away that caused further deaths.

core_ideas.concept: Nuclear Is the Safest Form of Energy
core_ideas.explanation: Three Mile Island killed no one. At Fukushima, people died from the tsunami and the rushed evacuation, not from radiation. Chernobyl did kill people, though the numbers are disputed. Even on the worst estimates, sixty years of nuclear power have killed fewer people than one month of coal-related accidents. France gets 71% of its power from nuclear, has had no safety issues and has low carbon emissions. Sixty years of nuclear waste would fit in an underground bunker the size of a Walmart.
core_ideas.quote: Nuclear energy is the safest form of energy known to man.

core_ideas.concept: Ideological Packages and the Environmentalist's Dissonance
core_ideas.explanation: Nuclear power and nuclear bombs are separate things. Twenty-four countries run nuclear power and have never built a bomb. The two got fused in the 1970s peace and environmental movements. Tribes adopt a bundle of dogmas and defend the whole bundle even when the facts change. The result is environmentalists who call climate change one of the great problems of our time but welcome solar and wind while banning nuclear.
core_ideas.quote: And how ideological tribes form is that they will take a package of dogmatic assertions and then they will stick to the entire package.

core_ideas.concept: The Three Distinct Sources of Nuclear Risk
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's first-principles breakdown has three parts. First, radioactive material behaves unlike anything in daily life: it travels thousands of kilometres, falls as radioactive rain and causes birth defects. Second, a runaway chain reaction can melt deep into the ground and contaminate groundwater. Third, a reactor is a complex system with nonlinear interactions, where small human errors can grow into catastrophes.
core_ideas.quote: So you don't have a simple causality. You have a complex system where many pieces are interacting. And then there can be unpredictable events that will come.

core_ideas.explanation: The real choice is to add some nuclear risk and remove some coal risk. Coal is the dirtiest source on pollution, carbon dioxide and deaths, before you even count climate change. Measured by deaths per megawatt-hour, nuclear wins. Our intuition gets this wrong for the same reason it gets planes and cars wrong: flying from Bombay to Delhi is far safer than driving, but plane crashes make headlines and car crashes don't.
core_ideas.quote: So it's the same kind of problem that a car accident doesn't make headlines. A plane accident makes headlines.

core_ideas.concept: Safety Is an Engineering Problem, Not a Fixed Fact
core_ideas.explanation: Ralph Nader's 'Unsafe at Any Speed' did not end cars; it set off huge gains in car safety. The three famous accidents all involved first-generation designs from when humanity was just starting out. Newer reactors shut themselves down when something goes wrong, with forces like gravity pulling the fissile material apart so no runaway reaction is possible. There is already proof that this works: the nuclear reactors on aircraft carriers and submarines have run for decades without incident in advanced economies.
core_ideas.quote: This is the heart of the idea that it's about clever engineering.

core_ideas.explanation: Chernobyl was a failure of decision-making inside an oppressive system where people were afraid to object. Societies with free speech, dissent and criticism notice when things go wrong and correct them. That is also why the Soviets never mastered aircraft carriers or submarines while advanced democracies did. Nuclear safety depends heavily on institutions.
core_ideas.quote: authoritarian systems make people stupid and they make mistakes

core_ideas.concept: Industrialise the Reactor: Small Modular Reactors
core_ideas.explanation: A 4,000 MW plant takes about twenty years to build and will only ever be made in a handful, so it never gets cheaper. A 50–100 MW small modular reactor, roughly the size of a big truck, could be made by the thousand on an assembly line. It would arrive in a crate and be switched on like a factory's diesel generator. By Ajay's rough maths, 50 MW serves about 25,000 households or runs a large factory. Solar's huge cost collapse came the same way, from two simple, scaled manufacturing steps: polysilicon made in about ten factories worldwide, then simple semiconductor processing. This is no longer just theory: Meta and Google have placed big SMR orders.
core_ideas.quote: How do you get the price of a nuclear reactor down? The answer is industrialization.

core_ideas.concept: Nuclear Power Is a Business, Not a Department
core_ideas.explanation: Separate weapons from energy, the way steel for artillery shells is a defence matter while steel for everything else is ordinary trade. India assumed everything nuclear belongs to the Department of Atomic Energy, and nuclear's share of India's energy has stayed minuscule and has not grown. Building reactors (L&T), running power plants (Tata Power, Reliance Energy) and buying captive power (Hindalco) should all be private business decisions, with competing imports, the way imported equipment competes with BHEL.
core_ideas.quote: It is congenitally not possible for the Indian State to do anything efficiently.

core_ideas.concept: The Evening Peak: Storage vs Nuclear as a Private Bet
core_ideas.explanation: Solar is unbeatable while the sun shines, but it sets just as people get home and switch on ACs, TVs and fridges. Once coal is gone, every evening brings a supply crunch and a price spike. Investors who think storage technology can handle it should build storage. Those who doubt it should build nuclear, which keeps running into the evening. Ajay says these should be speculative bets by private players, with no central planning.
core_ideas.quote: But the sun has an unpleasant habit of setting every evening.

core_ideas.concept: The Five Conditions for Nuclear Freedom in India
core_ideas.explanation: (1) Private Indians must be free to import nuclear plants. A 50 MW unit costs about $200–300 million, which India's top hundred companies can afford. (2) Plant owners must be free to sell power directly to industrial and commercial buyers, bypassing reluctant DISCOMs, as offshore wind developers can. (3) Security on the airport model: the CISF guards uranium and waste at private plants under clear protocols, paid for by the operator. (4) India must sign and comply with IAEA standards on fuel and waste so the world will sell it reactors and fuel. (5) Civil nuclear liability law must be fixed.
core_ideas.quote: Principle one, private people should be free.

core_ideas.explanation: Indian law makes the reactor vendor liable forever for any safety problem, so no global vendor will sell to India. The international doctrine works like a car: after the handover date, the operator is responsible. Victims sue only the operator, and the operator alone can sue the vendor if a design defect caused the accident.
core_ideas.quote: So I think we need to man up around this that like all other industrial equipment. There's a handover date, and then responsibility shifts to the operator.

core_ideas.concept: An Argument for Freedom, Not for Action
core_ideas.explanation: The hosts are not telling companies to invest in nuclear or telling the state to build it. They are asking only that the state stop blocking the choice. Amit adds a twist: if the government truly regulated for safety, it would mandate nuclear, and they don't want that either. Under freedom, private players will weigh solar, wind, storage and nuclear on their own business logic.
core_ideas.quote: We are not arguing for action. We are arguing for freedom, that this is incredible. Let's not shut it out with state action that gets in the way.

core_ideas.concept: Invisible Infrastructure and the Homeostasis of Debate
core_ideas.explanation: Amit worries that India lacks the invisible infrastructure, such as rule of law and mature processes, that makes this model work in the West. The state might hand the sector to a crony, botch security, or turn any small role into rent-seeking. Ajay admits the path will be difficult. His answer is a lively intellectual ecosystem of researchers, writers and critics that pulls a fumbling state back whenever it overshoots in either direction.
core_ideas.quote: The answer lies in knowledge and community that we need enough people in India who think, who write, who debate, who criticize.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: The opening: at a recent conference three different people walked up to Ajay and called him Amit. A rattled Ajay messaged Amit asking 'Do people call you Ajay?' Amit's reply: 'No, bro, never happened to me, must be something with you.'
Ajay announcing that 'all the great stories of the world begin at the second world war' before launching into the Battle of the Atlantic.
During the Battle of the Atlantic story the hosts reach for 'a Bob Dylan song' and sing their own version about how many ships the U-boats must shoot down 'before the British have no food.'
Ajay pitching the dream of small modular reactors: 'you just go buy an SMR off the shelf from DMart and you will plop it in your backyard and you've got a nuclear reactor up and running.'

Amit, after Ajay's case against artisanal production: 'this is an artisanal show. We are both artisans. If not artists, we can have delusions about that.' So it's ironic, he says, to hear Ajay say don't do important things the artisanal way.
Ajay's household power maths: a home draws about two thousand watts, but 'between friends, I'm gonna call it a thousand', because 'to do good oral calculations, we don't want pesky little details.'
Amit sizing a 50 MW reactor in Mumbai terms: 'not Andheri size, maybe Versova size, definitely Yari Road size.'

Ajay says the sun has 'an unpleasant habit of setting every evening.' Amit later corrects him in Hindi: 'Ki sir, sunset nahi ho raha, hum ghoom rahe' ('Sir, the sun isn't setting, we're the ones turning').

Amit turns the safety objection around: if the government really regulated nuclear power on safety grounds, 'they would immediately mandate that they get nuclear power. Because it is far safer than any other kind of power in use now.'

Amit says Patti Smith and Robert Mapplethorpe 'have in fact been compared to our crew, Nomsita Haritashya and Vaishnav Vyas, as these photographs will indicate. Is there a similarity or not? I leave it to you to decide.'
Ajay, a self-confessed 'old fogey' whose music is 'all ancient', marvels that he now loves a song made 'as recently as 2016.'
The sign-off: 'Where is your home, Ajay Shah? Your spiritual home, your intellectual home.' The answer: 'Bandra East.'

Ralph Nader's 'Unsafe at Any Speed' (1965), which documented the dangers of American cars. Ajay uses it to argue that exposing a technology's flaws leads to engineering fixes, not to abandoning the technology.
Meta (aka Facebook) and Google placing big orders for small modular reactors in practically the same week Ajay and Akshay Jaitly's article came out. Amit: 'We are beyond the world of theory.'
